title: When a Vocab Platform Cares More About Time in App and Tracking Student Clicks Than Real Learning
author: Dr. Nidhi Gupta
summary: In a guest essay for Emily Cherkin's First Fish Chronicles, pediatrician Dr. Nidhi Gupta examines Membean, a vocabulary platform used in more than 40,000 classrooms, after students told her they disliked it enough to forfeit grades. She finds that participation and grades are tied to minutes logged, typically 30 per week across at least three sessions, rather than accuracy or mastery. The platform also tracks student activity in detail, and she asks who can see those records and for how long. She questions the educational value of some challenges, such as inventing a slang word, and the developmental fit of some content. Her larger point is that no one clearly vets the student-facing content of school-assigned EdTech, since parents know the names, teachers know the features, and leaders weigh cost and convenience. She closes with six questions schools should answer before adopting a platform and asks readers whose schools use Membean to contact her.
points: Grading by time online confuses seat time with mastery and penalizes students who learn quickly.
Detailed click tracking raises unanswered questions about who accesses student data and how long it is kept.
Responsibility for vetting student-facing EdTech content falls through the gaps between parents, teachers and school leaders.
Schools should ask about content review, learning evidence, data retention, grading basis, parent preview and non-digital alternatives before adopting a platform.
quotes: Student participation and grades are tied to completing these minutes rather than to accuracy or demonstrating vocabulary mastery.
Should the number of minutes a child spends on an online platform determine their academic grade?
Of course, repetition and practice help strengthen learning. But time spent practicing isn’t necessarily evidence of mastery.
While students work through the material, Membean records their activity in considerable detail, stating clearly, “If they log in, we track them.
Parents recognize the names of these platforms without ever seeing what happens inside them.
School leaders may evaluate cost and convenience without fully examining the student experience.

Honestly, parents and educators shouldn’t have to conduct their own investigations to understand what children encounter through school-assigned technology. Just because everyone else is using it does not automatically make it educational, safe, or developmentally appropriate.

I’m not asking schools to reject technology. I’m asking them to examine it more carefully– not as an advocate for or against technology, but through the eyes of a 10- or 14-year-old child who encounters this content repeatedly.
